[Thinking]
**Crafting a ghost story**

I’m thinking about crafting a ghost story set in ancient China, and I want to keep the length moderate. I’ll focus on creating an eerie atmosphere while weaving in cultural elements. Maybe I could explore themes of tradition, loss, or even justice! I need to make sure the characters are compelling and that the plot has a nice twist. I’m excited to dive into this creative process! Let's build something intriguing!
[/Thinking]

The moon over the Wei River was thin as a blade on the night Magistrate Liang took the old road.

He had been warned against it.

At the last village before the pass, an innkeeper with a scar across his brow had set down a bowl of millet wine and said, “My lord, the southern road is longer, but it is a road for living men.”

Liang had looked up from his travel papers. “And the old road?”

The innkeeper’s eyes went to the shuttered window, though no wind stirred outside. “That road belongs to the Lantern Bride.”

The servants behind Liang crossed themselves in the old village fashion, touching brow, lips, and heart. One whispered a charm to the Kitchen God.

Liang was a magistrate of the Qin commandery, a man trained in law, measures, punishments, and grain tallies. He did not believe in village nonsense. He believed in seals stamped in red ink and witnesses who could be beaten until truth fell out of them like grain from a torn sack.

“I must reach Chang’an before the first day of the month,” he said. “We take the old road.”

The innkeeper bowed and did not argue. But when Liang rose before dawn, two of his servants had fled.

Only his clerk, young Shen, remained, pale and unhappy, clutching the magistrate’s document box as if it were a shield.

The old road ran between black pines and abandoned fields, past crumbling shrines where moss had eaten the faces of stone guardians. It had once carried silk, lacquer, tea, soldiers, brides, taxes, and coffins. Now grass grew between the paving stones, and the wheel ruts were filled with water though it had not rained in ten days.

By sunset, mist rose from the ground.

“My lord,” Shen said softly, “do you hear music?”

Liang pulled his cloak tighter. “It is the wind in the bamboo.”

“There is no bamboo.”

The magistrate stopped.

From ahead came the faint chiming of bells. Not temple bells—smaller, sweeter, like ornaments sewn into silk sleeves. A woman’s voice floated through the trees, singing words too old or too distant to understand.

Then the lantern appeared.

It hung in the mist, red as fresh blood, swaying though no hand held it. Behind it emerged a procession: bearers in wedding robes, musicians with flutes pressed to their lips, maidservants carrying lacquer boxes. Their garments were elegant but strangely out of fashion, with wide sleeves and high collars like figures painted on ancient tomb walls.

At the center stood a bridal sedan chair.

Its curtains were scarlet. Gold thread shimmered upon them in the pattern of paired mandarin ducks.

Shen gave a strangled cry and dropped to his knees.

Liang’s mouth went dry, but pride kept him upright. He stepped into the road and shouted, “Who travels here? I am Liang Wen, magistrate of Xianyang. Speak your business.”

The procession halted.

The music ceased all at once.

For a long moment there was only mist, the wet gleam of stones, and the red lantern burning without flame.

Then the curtains of the bridal chair parted.

A woman stepped down.

She wore a wedding robe the color of cinnabar, embroidered with phoenixes. Her hair was piled high and pinned with jade combs. Over her face hung a veil of red silk, thin enough to show the pale curve of her chin and lips as dark as crushed mulberries.

She bowed.

“My lord magistrate,” she said, and her voice was as gentle as water poured into a cup. “You travel late.”

Liang found his courage returning. Ghost or bandit, all things under Heaven had names and causes. “And you travel on a government road without permit.”

A whisper moved through the procession.

The bride laughed softly.

“I have been waiting for a government official,” she said. “Perhaps Heaven has sent one at last.”

Shen trembled. “My lord, we should go. We should go now.”

Liang ignored him. “What grievance do you claim?”

The bride turned her veiled face toward the dark fields. “Three hundred years ago, I was called Lin Mei. My father was a minor noble ruined by taxes and war. To save our household, he married me to Lord Han of the western valley, a man old enough to be my grandfather.”

“Common enough,” Liang said.

“Yes,” she replied. “Common things are often the cruelest.”

The red lantern swayed.

“I loved another,” she said. “A poor scholar named Wu Sheng. On the night before my wedding, he came to the old bridge and begged me to run away. I refused. I was dutiful. I was filial. I chose my father’s honor over my own heart.”

Her hands folded before her sleeves.

“The next day, my bridal procession took this road. Bandits came from the pines. They killed the bearers. They cut down the musicians. They dragged me from the chair and tore the gold pins from my hair.”

The mist thickened. Around the bridal party, Liang saw now what he had not seen before: throats gashed open, sleeves dark with old blood, faces gray beneath powder.

“I escaped to the bridge,” Lin Mei said. “There I found Wu Sheng hanging from the willow tree. He had died before dawn.”

Shen whimpered.

“I threw myself into the river,” the bride continued. “But the river would not take me. My body was found among the reeds. My spirit returned to the road. Since then, every year on the night of my wedding, I wait.”

“For what?” Liang asked, though he no longer wished to know.

“For a magistrate to hear my case.”

The words struck him more sharply than any cry.

Liang swallowed. “The bandits are dust. The lord you were to marry is dust. Your father is dust. No punishment can reach them.”

The bride tilted her head. “Are you certain?”

At once the mist split open.

The road changed.

The pines were gone. Dawn burned red over the hills. The bridal procession stood alive again, bright and laughing. Lin Mei’s veil fluttered in a spring wind. Musicians played. Men called blessings.

Then shadows moved among the trees.

Bandits descended with curved knives.

Liang watched men die. He saw a musician clutch his opened belly. He saw a maidservant fall with an arrow in her cheek. He saw Lin Mei dragged screaming from the sedan chair.

And among the bandits stood a man in an official’s dark robe, holding a ledger.

Liang stared. “Who is that?”

The vision shifted closer.

The official’s face was sharp, narrow-eyed, with the same mole beside the mouth that Liang saw each morning reflected in bronze.

Shen cried out, “My lord—it looks like you!”

“No,” Liang whispered.

The bride’s voice came from beside him. “Your ancestor, Liang Zhao. Magistrate of this district. He learned that Lord Han carried bridal gifts of gold, jade, and silk. He hired men to attack the procession, then recorded the crime as the work of nameless mountain thieves.”

Liang’s heart hammered.

The vision changed again.

He saw the ancient magistrate count gold beneath lamplight. He saw him hide jade combs in a lacquer chest. He saw him stamp a false report with the red seal of office.

Then he saw Lin Mei’s corpse lifted from the reeds, hair spread like river weed, wedding robe heavy with mud.

The bride raised one sleeve. In her pale hand lay a jade comb carved with phoenix wings.

“This was buried in your family shrine,” she said. “Beside the tablets of your honored dead.”

Liang remembered the comb. As a child he had seen it during ancestor rites, wrapped in yellow silk, said to be a reward granted by the First Emperor himself.

His knees weakened.

“What do you want?” he asked.

“Justice.”

“The guilty man is dead.”

“His bones lie in honor. His descendants rise in office. His name is spoken with incense.” Her voice hardened, and the mist grew cold enough to frost Liang’s beard. “Mine was written as foolish bride, drowned by shame.”

Liang could not meet her hidden eyes.

“What must I do?” he said.

The bride lifted her hand toward the north. “Return to Xianyang. Open the ancestral shrine of the Liang clan. Take the jade comb and the hidden ledger beneath the third stone. Bring them to the governor. Record the truth. Strip Liang Zhao’s name from the temple tablets. Build graves for those murdered on this road. Burn offerings not to silence us, but to remember us.”

“And if I refuse?”

The red lantern dimmed.

The procession turned their dead faces toward him.

From the bridal chair came a wet sound, like a body dragged from a river.

Lin Mei stepped closer. The veil stirred though there was no wind, and Liang saw beneath it not a maiden’s face but something pale and swollen, with river mud in its mouth and black fish moving behind its eyes.

“Then you will travel with us,” she whispered, “until another magistrate comes.”

Liang fell to his knees.

“I swear it,” he said. “By Heaven, by Earth, by the spirits of my ancestors, I swear.”

The bride regarded him in silence.

Then she reached out and touched his brow with two cold fingers.

The world went dark.

At dawn, Shen found Magistrate Liang lying beside the old bridge. His hair, black the night before, had turned entirely white. In his clenched hand was a strip of red silk embroidered with phoenixes.

They returned to Xianyang.

Three days later, Liang broke open the ancestral shrine before his horrified relatives. Beneath the third stone he found a bronze box green with age. Inside lay a ledger, brittle but legible, listing payments to men whose names matched criminals executed long ago. Wrapped beside it was the jade comb.

The governor, astonished and fearful, ordered the records corrected.

Liang Zhao’s tablet was removed from the Hall of Worthy Ancestors and burned outside the city wall. A stone was raised on the old road naming Lin Mei, Wu Sheng, the bearers, musicians, and maidservants who had died there. Graves were dug though no bones remained. Offerings of rice, wine, and paper lanterns were made for forty-nine nights.

On the last night, Magistrate Liang went alone to the bridge.

The moon was thin again.

Mist lay over the river.

For a long while nothing happened.

Then, across the water, a red lantern appeared. It did not sway this time. It floated steady and bright.

Behind it stood the bridal procession, no longer gray and torn, but whole. The musicians held their flutes. The bearers lifted the sedan chair. Maidservants smiled through tears.

Lin Mei stood upon the bridge.

Beside her was a young scholar in a plain robe, his hand in hers.

She bowed to Liang.

“My case is closed,” she said.

Liang bowed until his forehead touched the cold stone.

When he looked up, the bridge was empty.

Only the red lantern remained, drifting upward into the dark, higher and higher, until it became indistinguishable from the stars.

Years later, travelers once again used the old road. They said that on misty nights one might hear wedding music near the bridge, but no one feared it anymore. Sometimes a lost traveler would see a red lantern glowing ahead, guiding him safely through the pines.

And in the records of Xianyang, written in Magistrate Liang’s own hand, there remained a final note beneath the case of Lin Mei:

“When the dead cry out, it is not always for vengeance. Sometimes they ask only that the living tell the truth.”
